title: Chapter 14 — Nantucket
paragraphs: Nothing else noteworthy happened during the crossing, so after a fine run, we arrived safely in Nantucket.

Nantucket! Pull out your map and look at it. See what a real corner of the world it occupies — way offshore, lonelier than the Eddystone lighthouse. A mere hillock, an elbow of sand, all beach without a background. There's more sand there than you'd use in twenty years as blotting paper. Jokers will tell you they have to plant weeds because nothing grows naturally, that they import Canadian thistles, that they send overseas for a wooden plug to stop a leak, that wood is carried around like relics of the True Cross in Rome, that people plant toadstools for shade in summer, that one blade of grass makes an oasis and three blades a prairie, that they wear quicksand shoes like Lapland snowshoes, and that they're so enclosed by the ocean that small clams sometimes attach to their chairs and tables, as barnacles cling to sea turtles. But these exaggerations only prove that Nantucket is no Illinois.

Consider the wonderful legend of how the island was first settled by the Native Americans. An eagle swooped down on the New England coast and carried off an infant in its talons. With loud cries the parents watched their child disappear over the wide water. They resolved to follow. Setting out in canoes, after a dangerous crossing they discovered the island — and there they found an empty ivory casket: the poor little skeleton.

No wonder, then, that these Nantucketers, born on a beach, took to the sea for a living! First they caught crabs and clams in the sand. Growing bolder, they waded out with nets for mackerel. More experienced, they pushed off in boats for cod. And at last, launching a navy of great ships, they explored the watery world, put an unbroken belt of voyages around it, peeked through the Bering Strait, and in all seasons and all oceans declared everlasting war on the mightiest living creature that has survived the Flood — the most monstrous, most mountainous beast! That Himalayan, salt-sea mastodon, clothed with such tremendous unconscious power that its very panics are more dangerous than its most malicious attacks!

And so these naked Nantucketers, these sea hermits, swarming from their anthill in the ocean, have overrun and conquered the watery world like so many Alexanders — dividing the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans among themselves the way three pirate powers divided Poland. Let America annex Mexico and pile Cuba on top of Canada; let England swarm across all India and hang its banner from the sun — two-thirds of this watery globe belong to the Nantucketer. The sea is his; he owns it as emperors own empires. Other sailors have only a right of passage. Merchant ships are merely floating bridges; warships are floating forts; even pirates, though they live on the sea the way highwaymen live on the road, only plunder other ships — other fragments of land like themselves — without drawing their living from the bottomless deep itself. The Nantucketer alone lives and revels on the sea. He alone, in the Bible's words, goes down to it in ships, plowing it back and forth as his private plantation. There is his home; there lies his business — a business that Noah's flood couldn't interrupt even if it drowned all of China. He lives on the sea as prairie chickens live on the prairie. He hides among the waves, he climbs them like chamois hunters climb the Alps. For years he doesn't see land, and when he finally reaches it, it smells like another world — stranger than the moon would seem to an Earthling. Like the landless gull that folds its wings at sunset and is rocked to sleep between the swells — so at nightfall the Nantucketer, out of sight of land, furls his sails and lies down to rest, while under his very pillow rush herds of walruses and whales.
